title: Latency-sensitive code patterns and defensive API contract guidelines
author: Ellie Thompson
content:
Summary:

This document prescribes coding patterns, API contract conventions, and lightweight runtime controls for latency-sensitive code paths in Redwood services. It is intended for engineers who own request/response-facing services (API gateways, model-adapter services, router/proxy layers and hot execution paths inside the serving runtime). The guidance focuses on predictability, fast failure, observability, and safe rollout of changes that could affect user-facing latency or cause cascading resource pressure.

Goals:
- Reduce tail latency risk through defensive coding and contracts.
- Make failures predictable and observable so automated SLO enforcement and rollbacks are reliable.
- Provide a small set of standardized patterns that teams can adopt incrementally.

Scope:
- Applies to any service handling synchronous requests with user-perceivable latency (hosted API endpoints, inter-service RPC on critical paths).
- Does NOT mandate language-level style rules beyond the patterns shown (examples in Go and Python).

Principles:
1) Prefer fail-fast to slow-fail in user-facing paths. Early rejection keeps systems stable and reduces unpredictable queuing.
2) Make intent explicit in contracts: timeouts, retry semantics, priority, and cost-estimate headers.
3) Observe before optimizing: attach lightweight metrics and traces at decision points (reject, queue, hedged request, fallback).
4) Keep production defaults conservative; make opt-in for aggressive latency optimizations.

API Contract Conventions:
- Required headers/metadata on public and internal sync endpoints:
  - X-Request-Priority: low|normal|high (default: normal)
  - X-Request-Timeout-ms: integer (server must honor if <= configured max)
  - X-Client-Estimated-Cost: numeric (optional, used for routing/cost-aware decisions)
- Timeouts are part of the contract. Handlers must declare and honor a server-side deadline derived from X-Request-Timeout-ms or a service default.
- Retry semantics must be documented per-route with explicit idempotency classification. Non-idempotent mutating routes should not be auto-retried.

Recommended Patterns (high level):
1) Pre-emptive rejection (fast path): maintain a bounded request queue and reject when queue depth exceeds threshold. Rejection response: 503 with body {"error":"temporarily_unavailable", "retry_after_ms": 200}.
2) Circuit breaker per downstream dependency: open on sustained error budget breach or increased p99 latency, and return a clear error code (e.g., 502 with reason=downstream_circuit_open).
3) Hedging for high-variance dependencies: issue a second (hedged) request after a short delay (e.g., 40ms) when p95 > target. Limit to 1 additional hedge.
4) Async offload for best-effort work: push logs, metrics aggregation, and non-critical post-processing to background workers with durable queues.
5) Cancellation-aware code: propagate cancellation tokens/context and stop work ASAP to free CPU/GPU resources.
6) Backpressure propagation: map rejection signals to upstream clients where possible (HTTP 503 + Retry-After / gRPC RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED).
7) Lightweight adaptive batching: for GPU inference adapters, allow micro-batches up to a tight time window (e.g., 8ms) but expose an opt-out header for latency-critical requests (X-No-Batch: true).

Concrete implementation checklist (engineers):
1) Add server-side deadline enforcement at the top of each request handler: read X-Request-Timeout-ms, clamp to service_max_timeout_ms.
2) Implement bounded queueing with meter: track queue_depth, enqueue_latency_ms_histogram, rejections_count.
3) Instrument points of decision: rejection, circuit_open, hedge_sent, fallback_used, batch_flush.
4) Implement per-dependency circuit breaker with simple state machine and ramp-down action (fail closed -> fast path fallback) and periodic half-open probes.
5) Default behavior: on overload, return 503 and increment overload_slo_breach counter; do not block trying to satisfy slow requests.

Example config table (recommended defaults):
| key | default | rationale | owner |
|-----|---------|-----------|-------|
| service_max_timeout_ms | 5000 | hard upper bound; protects downstream and compute pools | service-owner |
| default_request_timeout_ms | 1000 | typical user-facing endpoint p95 target 300ms, default timeout gives headroom | service-owner |
| max_queue_depth | 128 | prevents unbounded memory growth; tune by qps/cpu | service-owner |
| reject_queue_threshold | 96 | start rejecting before queue is full to preserve headroom | service-owner |
| hedging_initial_delay_ms | 40 | small hedge window for high-variance ops | infra/perf |
| hedging_max_extra_requests | 1 | limit the multiplier to contain cost | infra/perf |
| circuit_breaker_error_rate_pct | 30 | open circuit when > 30% errors in rolling window | service-owner |
| probe_half_open_interval_s | 30 | periodic check to recover from open state | service-owner |

(Represented above as a simple ASCII table; use the config service to store authoritative values.)

Code snippets:
1) Go: context-aware handler + bounded queue rejection

```go
func Handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    ctx := r.Context()
    deadline := serverDeadlineFromHeaders(r.Header)
    ctx, cancel := context.WithDeadline(ctx, deadline)
    defer cancel()

    if !tryEnqueue() { // non-blocking check
        w.Header().Set("Retry-After", "0.2")
        http.Error(w, "temporarily_unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        metrics.Rejections.Inc()
        return
    }
    defer dequeue()

    // do work, always check ctx.Done()
    select {
    case result := <-doWorkAsync(ctx):
        writeJSON(w, result)
    case <-ctx.Done():
        // cancelled or timed out
        http.Error(w, "deadline_exceeded", http.StatusGatewayTimeout)
    }
}
```

2) Python (asyncio): hedging pattern example

```python
import asyncio

async def call_downstream(ctx, payload):
    # library call that honors ctx timeout
    return await httpx.post(..., timeout=ctx.timeout)

async def handle(req):
    timeout = min(req.headers.get('X-Request-Timeout-ms', 1000), 5000) / 1000
    ctx = RequestContext(timeout=timeout)

    first = asyncio.create_task(call_downstream(ctx, req.body))
    # schedule a hedge after short delay
    await asyncio.sleep(0.04)
    second = asyncio.create_task(call_downstream(ctx, req.body))

    done, pending = await asyncio.wait([first, second], return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
    for p in pending:
        p.cancel()
    return done.pop().result()
```

Operational runbook (summary):
1) Signals to watch: rising p95/p99, queue_depth > reject_threshold, rejections/sec, circuit_open_count, cost_per_request.
2) Immediate mitigation steps:
   a) Disable hedging (feature flag) if it increases cost under overload.
   b) Lower batch window for batched adapters.
   c) Increase autoscaler target for dedicated pools (if available).
   d) Enable more aggressive rejection (reduce reject_queue_threshold) as a short-term safety valve.
3) For persistent degradation: rollback recent commits that changed batching/serialization/DB query patterns; escalate to platform SRE.

Rollout and testing guidance:
- Feature-flag all new defensive patterns (circuit breaker parameters, hedging, queue size changes).
- Canary rollout to 5% of traffic with synthetic traffic that exercises high tail latency scenarios.
- Validate observability: ensure metrics emitted and traces correlate decision points within 1 hour of canary.
- Run a small load test that increases p95 to target to confirm hedging/circuit open behavior.

SLO and measurement recommendations:
- Service-level: p95 < 300ms, p99 < 800ms for normal-priority requests. Document per-service deviations.
- Error budget: maintain <1% error budget burn per week from overload rejections. Track rejections as first-class SLI.
- Cost monitoring: track extra_requests/total_requests and cost_per_thousand to quantify hedging overhead.

Ownership and escalation:
- Service owner: responsible for choosing defaults from the recommended config and validating customer impact.
- Platform/perf: owns hedging libraries, circuit-breaker primitives, and default telemetry.
- SRE on-call: escalation path for sustained p99 violations: page SRE, run the Operational runbook steps, and coordinate rollback with service owner.

Decision record (short form):
- Decision: Adopt bounded-queue + reject-first safety model with optional hedging and circuit breakers.
- Rationale: Protect limited GPU/CPU resources from unbounded queuing and provide deterministic failure semantics.
- Alternatives considered: unlimited queueing + aggressive autoscaling (rejected due to cost and unpredictability), synchronous backpressure propagation only (insufficient when upstream clients cannot react).

References and related docs:
- See performance SLO guide and runtime-serving-modes doc for how service latency targets are set.
- See observability-standards for metric naming, histogram buckets, and trace correlation keys.

Appendix: Metric names (recommended):
- service.queue_depth (gauge)
- service.rejects_total (counter)
- service.hedges_total (counter)
- downstream.<dep>.circuit_open (gauge/boolean)
- service.request_latency_ms (histogram)

Questions & next steps:
- Teams should run a single-week experiment to apply these patterns to one critical endpoint and report results at the monthly performance review.
- Platform team will provide a library implementing queueing/circuit/hedging primitives by Q2 2026.
